intro: Cordoba keeps its oldest trees behind walls. The city's public gardens were laid out in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, so its own catalogue of singular trees is full of magnificent specimens only eighty or ninety years old, while the genuinely ancient ones stand in a cathedral courtyard and a palace garden. What the city has in abundance is scale and scent: a plane reaching thirty-seven metres, another split in half by a cyclone and still standing, and a courtyard of bitter oranges watered by the same channels for centuries.
meta_description: Cordoba's oldest tree is an olive drawn on a 1741 plan and still fruiting on half a trunk. That, a 400-year holm oak, and the orange courtyard.
question_meta: Cordoba's oldest tree is the olive in the Mezquita's orange courtyard, on a 1741 plan and still bearing 60 kilos a year on half a trunk.
question_answer: The oldest tree in Cordoba is the olive beside the fountain in the Patio de los Naranjos, the orange courtyard of the Mezquita-Catedral. It already appears on a plan of the courtyard drawn in 1741, which makes it around 285 years old, and it is documented rather than estimated. The Patio is free to enter daily, so this is one ancient tree that costs nothing to stand in front of.
question_context: Half of its trunk is gone. The tree hollowed through the twentieth century and decayed badly from the 1980s, so what leans toward the fountain today is a shell that still produces about sixty kilos of olives a year, and the cathedral chapter has planted a young olive nearby as its eventual successor. In 2018 researchers sampled its leaves and fruit without harming it and found a local cultivar barely recorded anywhere else, which they have proposed naming after the city. Tourist copy sometimes calls the tree a thousand years old; there is no basis for that, and the 1741 plan is the actual evidence. The only tree in Cordoba that may be older is the holm oak in the garden of the Palacio de Viana, which the palace says has stood for four centuries and which rises above the roofline at over twenty-five metres, though that age rests on the palace's own word rather than on any survey. Everything else in the city is younger than it looks.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Cordoba?
faq.a: The olive beside the fountain in the Patio de los Naranjos, around 285 years old and documented on a 1741 plan of the courtyard. It survives on half a trunk and still fruits. Free to visit, daily.

faq.q: When does the orange blossom in Cordoba?
faq.a: The azahar peaks in late March and early April, and the scent lasts roughly a month on the tree. The exact date shifts every year with the weather, so nobody can promise you a week.

faq.q: Does Cordoba have really ancient trees?
faq.a: Two, honestly. The rest of the city's remarkable trees are eighty to a hundred and thirty years old, because its public gardens were laid out in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. Several of them are spectacular anyway.

faq.q: Which of these are free to see?
faq.a: All but two. The Patio de los Naranjos with its olive, the Orive garden, the Agriculture Gardens, the Alpargate plane and the cemetery Judas tree cost nothing. The Viana holm oak is inside a paid museum.

trees.name: The Olive of the Orange Courtyard

location.address: Patio de los Naranjos, Mezquita-Catedral, Calle del Cardenal Herrero, 14003 Cordoba

trees.story: This tree is on a map drawn in 1741, which is a rarer thing than being old. Most claims about an ancient tree's age come from tradition; this one comes from an inventory of the courtyard that counted, alongside the olive, ninety-five orange trees, six cypresses, ten palms and a chinaberry. Two and a half centuries later roughly half its trunk is gone. It hollowed through the twentieth century, decayed badly from the 1980s, and what leans toward the fountain now is a shell that still manages about sixty kilos of olives a year. The cathedral chapter has conserved what remains and planted a young olive nearby to take over eventually. In 2018 researchers took leaf and fruit samples without harming it and found a cultivar barely recorded anywhere else, which they have proposed naming after the city. The fountain beside it is officially the Fuente de Santa Maria, finished in December 1741, but everyone calls its spout the Cano del Olivo, after the tree. Suitors were once told to drink from it for luck in love.
trees.access: Free, the Patio de los Naranjos is open daily 08:30 to 19:00 (the prayer hall is ticketed separately)
trees.transport: In the historic centre, a few minutes on foot from anywhere in the old town
trees.notes: Age is documented rather than estimated: the tree appears on a 1741 plan of the courtyard, corroborated by the municipal singular-trees catalogue and by regional television reporting the 2018 DNA study. Tourist sources calling it 'almost a thousand years old' have no documentary basis and are not used here.

best_time.label: September to November: the harvest, when the fruit turns from green to black

trees.name: The Orange Courtyard of the Mezquita
trees.age_estimate: a grove documented since 1512, replanted tree by tree

location.address: Patio de los Naranjos, Mezquita-Catedral, 14003 Cordoba

trees.story: Ninety-eight bitter orange trees stand here in rows that line up with the columns of the prayer hall next door, so the courtyard reads as the building continuing outdoors into the light. It may be the oldest surviving garden in Europe: the enclosure goes back to the mosque founded in 784, orange trees are recorded in it from at least 1512, and the shallow channels that link the tree pits still carry the water that feeds them. In 2001 workers found a tenth-century cistern twelve metres beneath the paving, built to hold twelve hundred cubic metres so that washing and irrigation would never stop. Be honest about the trees themselves: they are ordinary Seville oranges, replaced one by one as they fail, so the grid is old and the individuals are not. What is worth timing a trip for is the last days of March, when the whole courtyard flowers at once and the scent of azahar carries out into the surrounding streets. Since 2026 the chapter has turned the bitter harvest, previously thrown away, into vinegar.
trees.transport: In the historic centre, on foot
trees.notes: An ensemble entry, and it passes the collectible-point test on purpose: a bounded courtyard of about 50 by 30 metres, planted in a deliberate grid, famous for being exactly that, with one obvious place to stand. The age range describes the individual trees, which are replaced as they fail; the grove itself is documented from 1512. The flowering window is real but shifts every year, so no week is claimed.

best_time.label: late March into April, when the whole courtyard flowers and the scent carries into the streets

trees.name: The Holm Oak of the Viana Palace
trees.age_estimate: said by the palace to be over 400 years

location.address: Palacio de Viana, Plaza de Don Gome 2, 14001 Cordoba

trees.story: Twelve courtyards, eighteen noble families, five centuries of owners, and the oldest inhabitant of the house is a tree. The palace calls this holm oak four hundred years old, which would make it older than most of the building around it, and at over twenty-five metres it rises clear above the roofline, so you see it from the street before you have paid to go in. It stands in the middle of a garden that only became a garden in 1814, when the seventh Marquis of Villaseca bought the land and laid it out in the French manner with sixteen box parterres that are themselves two centuries old now. Against the walls grow espaliered lemon, lime, mandarin, orange and grapefruit, the oldest plants in the palace after the oak itself. A holm oak is an evergreen, so there is no season to catch it in: the leaves are small, dark and leathery, closer to an olive's than to the lobed oak leaf on an English pub sign, and they stay all year. Worth knowing before you go: the four-century figure rests on the palace's own account, with no forestry survey behind it.
trees.access: Paid entry to the Palacio de Viana museum; closed Mondays, shorter hours in July and August
trees.transport: About 15 min walk northeast of the Mezquita
trees.notes: Two published sources give the same 400-year figure and both very likely trace to the palace museum itself; no press, botanical or register source dates it independently. Published as the palace's claim rather than as established fact. Pin is the garden, not a surveyed trunk position.

trees.name: The Jacaranda of the Orive Garden

location.address: Jardines de Orive, Plaza de Orive, 14002 Cordoba

trees.story: For four hundred years nobody outside could see this tree. It grew in a walled orchard belonging first to a Dominican convent, on ground granted in 1241, and then to a Renaissance palace built in 1560 by the architect Hernan Ruiz II, and the gate was only opened to the public in 2004. It has come close to dying twice since. Naturalists recording it note that it barely survived the freeze of 2003, when Cordoba hit nine degrees below zero, and the municipal catalogue records the winters of 2010 and 2011 killing jacarandas across the city while this one held on. What stands there now is three trunks grown together into what looks like one tree, spreading a crown twenty metres across at nearly nineteen metres tall, probably the largest of its kind in the city. For most of the year it is a fine green canopy over a quiet square. For a couple of weeks in May it turns violet, flowering largely before the new leaves arrive, which is the whole reason jacarandas were planted across southern Spain in the first place.
trees.transport: About 12 min walk northeast of the Mezquita
trees.notes: The municipal catalogue says dating tests suggest it could be centenarian but does not settle it, and notes it is almost certainly two or three individuals fused. The flowering month is sourced from southern Spain generally rather than from Cordoba specifically, so no precise week is claimed. Pin is the garden; the catalogue's longitude for this record was lost in text extraction and was substituted from a neighbouring tree in the same small garden.

best_time.label: May, when it turns violet before the new leaves arrive

trees.name: The Giant Plane of the Agriculture Gardens
trees.story: At thirty-seven metres this is the tallest tree in Cordoba's own catalogue of singular trees, and it stands in the city's oldest public garden, opened on the first of March 1811 by a mayor who had spent years travelling the Islamic world disguised as a Syrian prince. The trunk measures nearly four metres around and widens to over five at the base, which is what a plane does when nothing has hurried it. Cordobans do not call this place the Agriculture Gardens. They call it Los Patos, after the duck pond, and they have done so for generations. The tree rings a small central plaza together with several other big planes, so the one to look for is the tallest, the one whose crown disappears above the others when you stand underneath. The gardens were reorganised in 1864 and bought outright by the council in 1866, so the ground has been public for a hundred and sixty years, which in a city that keeps its best trees behind walls is worth something. A plane's autumn in Andalusia is a dull brown, so come for the size, not the season.
trees.transport: About 16 min walk northwest of the Mezquita
trees.notes: The municipal catalogue gives the dimensions and calls the age probably centenarian without dating it. Pin is the central plazoleta: this is the largest of a group of similar planes there, and no source distinguishes the individual by coordinate.

trees.name: The Split Plane of the Alpargate
trees.age_estimate: one of the oldest planes in the city

location.address: Plaza del Cristo de Gracia, 14002 Cordoba

trees.story: A cyclone tore this tree in half and it is still twenty-four metres tall. What stands over the Plaza del Cristo de Gracia today is the surviving portion of something that was once roughly twice the size, and the municipal catalogue rates it as very probably one of the oldest planes in Cordoba. Its crown occupies twenty of those twenty-four metres, so from beneath it there is essentially nothing else to see. It shades a Baroque fountain that the city paid for with the proceeds of three bullfights held in 1747, and which was moved to this square from the Puerta Nueva in 1950. During Holy Week the brotherhood of the Padres de Gracia carries its floats in and out beneath the branches, which is the one week of the year the tree has to make room for something. The catalogue's own photograph records a small indignity worth mentioning, because it says a lot about how cities treat their big trees: someone has bolted an electrical box to the trunk.
trees.transport: About 22 min walk northeast of the Mezquita
trees.notes: Undated: the municipal catalogue calls the age very advanced and says it is very probably among the oldest planes in Cordoba, without a figure. Sources disagree on species, one local site calling it an Oriental plane; the professional municipal catalogue's identification is used here.

trees.name: The Judas Tree of the San Rafael Cemetery
trees.age_estimate: undated, the largest of its species in the province

location.address: Cementerio de San Rafael, Avenida de Libia 2, 14005 Cordoba

trees.story: A tree that flowers straight out of its own bark, standing at the gate of a cemetery. Judas trees do not put their blossom on new shoots the way most trees do; the magenta flowers push directly through the old wood of the trunk and the heavy limbs, before any leaves appear, so for two or three weeks in early spring the whole frame of the tree is coloured rather than covered. Botanists recording Cordoba's remarkable trees name this one the largest specimen of its species in the province: two and three quarter metres around, though only ten metres tall, splitting into three arms below head height. It shares the entrance with a Mexican fan palm, two big red river gums and an uncommon jujube, in a cemetery that thousands of people walk through in the last days of October. Which is the wrong time to see it. Come in March instead, when the gate is quiet and the tree is doing the one thing it is famous for.
trees.access: Free, cemetery open from 08:30, closing 18:00 to 20:00 depending on season
trees.transport: About 20 min walk east of the Mezquita
trees.notes: No age published anywhere; the range is inferred from its dimensions and is the weakest figure on this page. The size claim (largest of its species in the province) comes from the municipal catalogue citing a botanical survey.

best_time.label: March and April, when magenta flowers push straight out of the bare bark

trees.name: The Cypress of the Alcazar Entrance

location.address: Outside the entrance, Alcazar de los Reyes Cristianos, Cordoba

trees.story:
Twenty-six and a half metres tall on a crown three and a half metres wide. That is a proportion closer to a lamp post than a tree, and it is what a Mediterranean cypress does when it is left to grow the way it wants: straight up, in one dark column, branches held so tight to the trunk that the whole thing reads as a single line.

It stands outside the ticket gate of the Alcazar de los Reyes Cristianos, which means it costs nothing to see. Everything else here is behind the wall and behind a turnstile: the long pools, the clipped hedges, the fortress Alfonso XI built in 1328, where Ferdinand and Isabella later held court and where the Inquisition ran its tribunal for three centuries. The cypress is the one thing the city left on the outside.

It is also young. Cordoba's catalogue of singular trees put it at about seventy-seven years when it was surveyed, and a register age is always the age on the day somebody wrote it down, so add whatever has passed since. That catalogue is the only source describing this tree at all. Cypresses run to several centuries, which makes this one barely started, and it is on the list anyway because of the shape rather than the years. Stand at the base and look up the column: there is almost nothing between you and the top of it.
trees.access: Free, outside the Alcazar's ticket gate
trees.transport: Centro Historico, next to the Alcazar; short walk from the Mezquita-Catedral

trees.name: The Siberian Elm of the Alcazar

location.address: Alcazar de los Reyes Cristianos, Cordoba

trees.story:
A Siberian elm is not supposed to reach twenty-seven metres. The species rarely passes fifteen, which is part of why it was planted across Spain in such numbers during the twentieth century: fast, cheap, indifferent to drought and poor soil, resistant to the Dutch elm disease that was destroying the country's field elms, and modest enough not to become a problem later. This one ignored the brief.

It grows inside the gardens of the Alcazar de los Reyes Cristianos, among the long water channels and clipped hedges laid out below the fortress, where nearly everything else is kept to a shape. The elm was allowed to run. Cordoba's catalogue of singular trees records its height and its species and nothing about its age, and no other source names it, so how it got here and when is simply not documented.

Reaching it costs money for most of the year, since the Alcazar charges admission, though on summer mornings the gardens are free. That is a real difference from the cypress standing outside the same gate, and worth knowing before you plan the walk.

Ulmus pumila comes from the steppe of northern China, Mongolia and eastern Siberia, ground where trees stay short because the wind and the drought keep them there. Give it Andalusian irrigation and a garden that never let it go without, and it turns into this.
trees.access: Paid entry (Alcazar gardens); free on summer mornings
trees.transport: Centro Historico, inside the Alcazar gardens; short walk from the Mezquita-Catedral

trees.name: The Himalayan Cedar of Plaza del Cardenal Toledo
trees.story:
The square was arranged around the tree. Plaza del Cardenal Toledo got its garden in 1945, and this deodar was already standing, so the paths and the benches went where the cedar allowed them. It remains effectively the only tree on the square, twenty-two and a half metres of it, which on a small plaza north of the Mezquita means it is also the roof.

Cordoba's catalogue of singular trees put it at about a hundred and two years old at survey, which is a floor rather than a figure, since it has gone on growing since somebody wrote that down. The catalogue is also the only source that says anything about this tree. Nothing else names it, which is ordinary for a square cedar and worth saying plainly rather than dressing up.

Cedrus deodara comes from the western Himalaya, from Afghanistan through Kashmir into Nepal, where it is a timber tree of high mountain forest and where the Sanskrit name means the wood of the gods. In Andalusia it is an ornamental, planted through the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries into gardens and new squares, and it does well as long as it is watered. The habit gives it away from a distance: a straight leader, branches sweeping down and out, every shoot tip drooping, so the whole tree looks like it is leaning slightly towards you.
trees.transport: Centro Historico; short walk north of the Mezquita-Catedral

trees.name: The Chinaberry of the Puerta de Almodóvar

location.address: Jardines de la Puerta de Almodóvar, beside the city gate, 14004 Córdoba
location.neighbourhood: Centro Histórico, beside the Alcázar walls

trees.story:
Four hundred square metres of shade, thrown by a species most cities plant as a modest street tree. Chinaberries usually stop somewhere around ten metres. This one is twenty-four and a half, which makes it less a tree in the gardens at the Puerta de Almodovar than the ceiling over them, and the reason people look up before they look at the gate.

Cordoba's own catalogue of singular trees measured it at about seventy-two years old, and a register age is the age on the day somebody wrote it down, so add what has passed since. That catalogue is the only source that has dated it. Local guides to the gate describe a giant cinamomo standing here, using the Spanish name for the species, which confirms the tree and what it is without confirming its years, so read the age as the city's estimate rather than a settled fact.

The gate beside it has six centuries on it either way. What stands today is a fourteenth-century Christian rebuild on the line of an older Arab gate, and the wall running from it towards the Alcazar is the one the tree grows against.

Melia azedarach came out of southern Asia and spread through Mediterranean cities for the shade and the lilac blossom, and its hard seed stones were strung as rosary beads, which is how the species picked up its other name of bead tree.
trees.access: Free, in the public gardens that surround the Puerta de Almodóvar city gate
trees.transport: Historic centre, a few minutes on foot from the Alcázar and the Mezquita

trees.name: The Ginkgo of the Agriculture Gardens

location.address: Jardines de la Agricultura (Jardín de los Patos), 14004 Córdoba

trees.story:
Every other tree in this garden has living relatives. This one has none. Ginkgo biloba is the only surviving species of an entire order of plants, and the fan-shaped leaf you pick up under it is the same shape found pressed into rock from two hundred million years ago.

Cordoba's catalogue of singular trees calls this the oldest ginkgo in the city's public gardens and put it at about seventy-two years when it was surveyed, a figure no independent source has ever checked. What other sources do confirm is which tree is meant: the garden's local history pages name it, and a geocache placed at its foot carries its name and is still listed as active, which is a small modern receipt that it is still standing.

The Jardines de la Agricultura opened in 1811 and nobody in Cordoba calls them that. They are Los Patos, after the duck pond. A ginkgo of seventy is barely started by the standards of a species that routinely passes a thousand years in China and Japan, so this is an early chapter rather than a veteran.

Come in late autumn. Ginkgo leaves turn a uniform gold and then release almost in unison, so the tree goes from lit to bare in a few days, and on the best of those days the gold is on the branches and on the ground at the same time.
trees.access: Free, public garden, popularly called the Jardín de los Patos
trees.transport: Historic centre / Ciudad Jardín, walking distance from Ronda de los Tejares

best_time.label: late November into early December, when the whole crown turns gold and drops within days

trees.name: The Casuarinas of the Plaza de Jerónimo Páez

location.address: Plaza de Jerónimo Páez, in front of the Archaeological Museum, 14003 Córdoba
location.neighbourhood: San Salvador y La Compañía, Centro Histórico

trees.story:
Three trees that read as pines from across the square and are not related to pines at all. What hangs off a casuarina in fine green threads is jointed twig, not needle; the leaves are reduced to rings of scales at each joint, the tree flowers, and the resemblance to a conifer is coincidence. In wind they hiss rather than rustle, which is why the species travels under the name whistling pine in half the countries that grow it.

The city's catalogue of singular trees registers three of them on this small plaza in front of the Archaeological Museum and puts the tallest above thirty metres. It gives no age, and no other source supplies one. An independent description of the square mentions its large casuarinas without measuring anything, which is as far as corroboration goes here, and the plaza was remodelled and refenced in stages that only finished in January 2011, so how much of what stands predates that work is genuinely open.

The ground under them is better dated than they are. The plaza takes its name from the Palacio de los Paez de Castillejo, now the Archaeological Museum, and beneath it lies a Roman theatre that an earthquake brought down in the third century.

The three grow close together against the museum wall, which makes them one sight with one place to stand rather than three separate errands.
trees.access: Free, open public plaza in the historic centre
trees.transport: Five minutes on foot from the Mezquita-Catedral

trees.name: The River Red Gum of the Celia Méndez Garden

location.neighbourhood: Distrito Sureste, roughly 3km east of the historic centre

trees.story:
The thickest trunk in Cordoba's catalogue of singular trees belongs to an Australian. This river red gum measures 4.86 metres around and stands 34.8 metres tall in a public park three kilometres east of the Mezquita, well outside the ring of old trees the city puts on its maps.

It is there because the ground used to be huertas, the irrigated market gardens that fed Cordoba along the Guadalquivir before the city grew east across them. The catalogue calls this tree a relict of those gardens. Eucalyptus camaldulensis follows watercourses in its own country and was planted across Spain in the twentieth century for that exact habit, cheap timber on wet ground, and this one outlived the reason it was put in.

One caution, plainly. The municipal catalogue is the only source that records this tree at all. Searching for it turns up a different and better-known Cordoba eucalyptus several kilometres away, so anyone checking online will most likely end up reading about the wrong one. The girth and the height are the city's own measurements and nobody has published a second set.

No age is on file, and none should be guessed. Red gums put on bulk fast where there is water, so five metres of trunk here does not imply centuries, and nothing in the record claims them.
trees.access: Free, public park (opening hours not confirmed)
trees.transport: Distrito Sureste, roughly 3km east of the historic centre; not within the existing 2.3km walk

trees.name: The Ash of Santa Marina
trees.age_estimate: argued to be over a century, not precisely dated

location.address: Plaza de Santa Marina, beside the north side of the Iglesia de Santa Marina de Aguas Santas, 14001 Córdoba

trees.story:
Somebody cut the top off this tree and it is still the largest ash in Cordoba. What stands on the north side of the church of Santa Marina is a heavy old trunk carrying thin, sparse regrowth and not much leaf, about nine and a half metres of it in total. By trunk perimeter it has been recorded as the biggest of its species in the city twice: in a 1984 book on Cordoba's trees, and again in the 2002 provincial inventory of singular trees.

The age is argued rather than documented. Rafa Tamajon, the local botanist who has written most about these trees, reads it as centenarian from its growth pattern and the history of the site, but there is no ring count and no planting record, so somewhere between one and one and a half centuries is as precise as anyone can honestly be. The trunk carries visible decay and the tree is described as declining. That is worth knowing, because it is the argument for going now rather than eventually.

Ash wants damp ground and Cordoba is not damp country, which is part of why one of this size got written down here at all.

A practical note: the sources place it on the plaza and on the church's north side, and that is as close as the pin goes. Walk the north wall and look for the big trunk under the small crown.

2002 provincial inventory of singular trees (Árboles y arboledas singulares de la provincia de Córdoba, Tamajón/Reyes/Sánchez Polaina)
